# Compound interest

## What interest is

Interest is the price of using money for a while. A saver who places money in an account lends it to the bank, and the bank pays a small fee for the privilege of holding it. A borrower does the opposite and pays the fee instead. The fee is usually written as a rate per year, such as four percent, so that people can compare offers without doing long sums. The amount first placed in the account is called the principal. Everything else in this topic follows from one simple question: what happens to the interest once it has been paid? If it is taken away and spent, the principal never changes. If it is left in the account, it joins the principal and starts to earn interest of its own. That second case is the subject of this lecture (slide 2, 1:10).

Before going further, it helps to fix a few words. The period is the length of time between two interest payments. The rate per period is the yearly rate divided by the number of periods in a year. The balance is whatever sits in the account at a given moment. With these three words in hand, every example in the lecture can be described in plain language, and most of the formulas become short and easy to read.

## Simple interest

Under simple interest the bank pays the same fee every year, always computed on the original principal. Suppose a saver deposits one thousand pounds at five percent a year. After the first year the account has earned fifty pounds. After the second year it has earned another fifty, and after ten years it has earned five hundred in total. The growth is a straight line: the same step is added again and again, and the size of the step never changes. Simple interest is easy to compute by hand, which is one reason it survives in short loans and in some bonds that pay a fixed coupon. Its weakness is that it ignores the interest already paid. Money that has been earned sits beside the principal but does no work, as if it were kept in a drawer at home (slide 4, 6:25).

## Compounding

Compound interest changes one rule. At the end of each period the interest is added to the balance, and the next payment is computed on the larger balance. Take the same deposit of one thousand pounds at five percent. After one year the balance is one thousand and fifty. In the second year the interest is five percent of that new figure, which is fifty two pounds and fifty pence rather than fifty. The extra amount looks tiny, but it repeats and grows every year. After ten years the balance is close to one thousand six hundred and twenty nine, so the saver has earned more than one hundred and twenty pounds beyond what simple interest would give. The growth is no longer a straight line but a curve that bends upward, because each step is a fixed share of a balance that keeps rising (slide 6, 12:40).

## Compounding more often

Banks do not always add interest once a year. Many add it every month or even every day. When the yearly rate is fixed, adding interest more often gives a slightly higher result, because each small payment starts earning sooner. A rate of twelve percent a year paid monthly means one percent each month, and over a year that grows a balance by about twelve point seven percent rather than twelve. The difference between the quoted rate and the rate actually earned is the reason lenders publish an annual equivalent rate. That figure turns every offer into a single yearly number, so a careful reader can compare a monthly product with a yearly one on fair terms (slide 9, 21:15).

There is a limit to this effect. As the periods become shorter and shorter, the gain from compounding more often becomes smaller and smaller. Moving from yearly to monthly payments makes a visible difference, but moving from daily payments to payments every second hardly changes anything. The limit is called continuous compounding, and it is the version most often used in finance textbooks, because it makes many later calculations neater.

## The rule of seventy two

A quick way to feel the power of compounding is the rule of seventy two. Divide seventy two by the yearly rate in percent, and the answer is roughly the number of years it takes for money to double. At six percent a balance doubles in about twelve years; at nine percent it doubles in about eight. The rule is not exact, but it is close for ordinary rates and it can be done in the head. It also works in reverse: if prices rise by three percent a year, the value of a fixed sum of cash falls by half in about twenty four years. The lecturer used this rule to warn that small differences in fees on a pension fund become large differences over a working life of forty years (slide 12, 30:05).

## Present value

Compounding runs forward in time, from today to some future date. The same idea can be run backward. If a payment of one thousand pounds will arrive in five years, what is it worth today? The answer is the amount that, invested now at the going rate, would grow to one thousand pounds by that date. This amount is called the present value, and the process of finding it is called discounting. At five percent a year the present value of that future payment is about seven hundred and eighty four pounds. Discounting lets an investor compare payments that arrive at different times, which is the core task of valuing bonds, loans and whole companies (slide 15, 41:30).

A useful habit is to draw a timeline before doing any sum. Mark today on the left, mark each payment at its date, and write the rate above the line. Then every question becomes either moving money forward with compounding or moving it backward with discounting.

## Common mistakes

Three mistakes came up again and again in past exam answers. The first is mixing a yearly rate with a monthly period without dividing the rate. The second is counting the number of periods wrongly, for example treating a loan that runs for three years with monthly payments as having three periods rather than thirty six. The third is forgetting that a quoted rate and an effective rate can differ, so that two offers which look identical on paper are not the same in practice. Each of these can be avoided by writing the rate and the period side by side before starting, and by checking that the units match (slide 18, 52:10).

## Summary

Compound interest adds each payment to the balance, so later payments are larger. More frequent compounding raises the effective rate, but with a clear limit. The rule of seventy two gives a fast estimate of doubling time, and discounting runs the same idea backward to give present values. Together these tools are enough for most everyday questions about savings, loans and investments, and they form the base for the more advanced valuation methods in the next lecture.
